full_judgment:
Zubayer Rahman Chowdhury J: Jail Appeal No. 1038 of 2004, at the instance of the condemned prisoner Hamidul, is directed against the order of conviction and sentence passed by the learned Additional Sessions Judge, 2nd Court, Naogaon in Sessions Case No.27 of 2002 under sections 302/341 109 of the Penal Code imposing the sentence of death upon him along with Helal and Saiful Islam, both absconding. Jail Appeal No. 1043 of 2004 was preferred by appellant Ashraf Ali Sheikh, who was convicted in the aforesaid case and sentenced to imprisonment for life along with a fine of Taka 5,000, in default, to suffer rigorous imprisonment for one year more. Absconding accused Shontosh Ali was, however, acquitted of the said charge. 

 3. The incident relates to a tragic and gruesome murder of an 8-year-old girl. The prosecution case is, that on 29-8-99 at about 7-00 PM in the evening, 8-year-old Setu hereinafter referred to as the deceased), daughter of Md Saidul Islam Chowdhury, went to take a wash from the tubewell. As she did not return home for some time, the informant made a search for her in the nearby vicinity, but she was not found. At that time, condemned prisoner Hamidul (hereinafter referred to as Hamidul) told the informant in presence of others that his daughter (the deceased) has been taken away by "Jin" (invisible force) and has been confined in the Doudpur Belbari School under some benches. The informant immediately went to the school where Fazlu Master opened the classrooms in order to search for the girl, but with no result. Upon their return from the school, the informant was once again told by Hamidul that his daughter was in the bamboo clump, located on the western side of his house. A search of that place proved futile as well. Thereafter, the informant and others made a search for the girl at various other places. 

 7. The police took up the case for investigation, visited the place of occurrence, prepared sketch map with index, inquest report and sent the dead body for postmortem examination which was conducted by Dr SA Faruque (PW 10). However, the postmortem report could not make any conclusive findings as to the cause of death since the dead body was highly decomposed. 

 16. On the other hand, the learned Assistant Attorney-General Ms Israt Jahan contended that since the confessional statement was true and voluntary and mutually consistent with the other evidence on record, the same can be relied upon to establish the implication of the condemned prisoners in the offence of murder. She further contends that mere omissions or discrepancies by itself will not cause any mischief to the prosecution case unless any glaring contradiction is found in the prosecution evidence. The learned Assistant Attorney-General has relied upon two decisions reported in AIR 1978 SC 1248 and 1988 Criminal Law Journal 24. 

 27. PW 6 Abu Sayed Chowdhury corroborated the informant in all material particulars. He denied the defence suggestion that the deceased was murdered in some other manner and that the case was initiated in order to deprive Hamidul from his landed property. 

 30. PW 9 Abdur Rahman was serving as the Sub-Inspector who recorded the FIR and conducted the investigation of the case. He visited the place of occurrence, prepared the inquest report and sent the dead body for post-mortem examination. He also seized alamats and prepared the seizure list which he identified as Exhibits. 3 and 4. He stated that both Hamidul and Ashraf were interrogated after their arrest and their statements were recorded under section 161 of the Code of Criminal Procedure. 

 39. Therefore, the prosecution version of the incident, placed in juxtaposition with the confessional statement of appellant Ashraf Ali Sheikh, deals a telling blow to the prosecution case. According to the prosecution witnesses, not only was Hamidul very much present at the village at the relevant time, the aforementioned witnesses had also spoken to him about the matter. On the other hand, according to the confessional statement, Hamidul and his associates, namely, Helal, Saiful and Ashraf Ali abducted the 8-year-old girl from near the tubewell just after sunset, took her first to the bamboo clump and then to Shamu's house at Khateshwar Mouza and thereafter, on that very night, to Hamidul-in-law's house at Horishpur village. Therefore, according to the confessional statement, on the fateful day, Hamidul was in the company of his associates from the time of occurrence just after sunset till well into the night. Apparently, the aforesaid two versions are mutually inconsistent, inasmuch as Hamidul could not have been present at two different places at the same time; this is not only improbable, but also impossible. 

 40. In the case of PC Gogoi vs State of Assam, reported in 1988 CrilJ 24, where the Court considered the decision reported in AIR 1978 SC 1248, it was held that where a confessional statement was corroborated by circumstances which indicated the same to be true and voluntary and was supported by the medical evidence on record, the conviction was perfectly valid. 

 41. The above mentioned decisions cited by the learned Assistant Attorney-General, which relate to a conviction being based upon confessional statement, is clearly distinguishable from the present case before us, inasmuch as in the aforesaid two decisions, the confessional statement made by the lone accused was inculpatory in nature and was fully corroborated by the prosecution witnesses as well as the medical evidence on record. In the instant case, it is far from that: not only is there no conclusive medical opinion as to the cause of death, the account of the incident as given out by the prosecution witnesses runs contrary to the confessional statement. In other words, if the prosecution witnesses' account of the incident is taken to be true, the confessional statement does not stand; on the other hand, if the confessional statement is taken to be true, it clearly negates the prosecution version of the incident. 

 42. In the case of Mizazul Islam @ Dablu vs State reported in 41 DLR (AD) 157, the inconsistent and contradictory version of the incident by the eyewitnesses, including the injured eye-witness, coupled with the contradiction in the confessional statement, led to the acquittal of the appellant. It would not, perhaps, be out of place to recount the facts of that case. The appellant was convicted under section 302 of the Penal Code and sentenced to death by the Sessions Judge, which was also confirmed by the High Court Division. The appellant, being a dismissed employee of PW 4, was alleged to have committed the act which resulted in the murder of PW 4's wife and also caused injury on the person of PW 4. It was the case of the prosecution that on the day of occurrence at about midnight, when the electric bulb outside PW 4's room went off, he came out and immediately, two persons, with their faces covered with scarf, appeared there and one of them gave a dagger blow on the chest of PW 4 and when his wife came forward to save him, she also received a dagger blow. Subsequently, the appellant came out from beneath the cot inside the room and was recognised by PW 4's wife (the deceased) and he inflicted dagger blows on both the deceased and PW 4. However, in his confessional statement, the appellant stated that when PW 4 opened the door, he stabbed him, while the other person stabbed the deceased. Addressing this issue, the Appellate Division held : 

 43. It is now well settled through judicial pronouncements that a confessional statement must not only be voluntary, but must be true as well in order to secure the conviction of the accused person. As has been held by the Supreme Court of India in the case of Sarwan Singh Rattan Singh vs State of Pun- jab, reported in AIR 1957 (SC) 637 : 

 "Even if the confession is held to be voluntary it must also to be established that the confession is true and it would be necessary to examine the confession and compare it with the rest of the prosecution evidence and the probabilities of the case." 

 44. In the case of Amir Hossain vs State reported in 37 DLR (AD) 139, the Apex Court allowed the appeal setting aside the conviction and held: 

 46. There is another aspect to this case. Apparently, a salish took place a day after the girl went missing which was attended by the informant, the Matbor, Member and other villagers where Hamidul admitted about the incident and undertook to bring out the girl after three days. We are baflled, to say the least, as to how Hamidul could be given 3 days' time to bring out the 8-year-old girl when she had already been missing for 24 hours. It is even more baflling that despite such admission by Hamidul, no information was given to the police and Hamidul was left to roam about freely for 3 days after which he decamped. 

 50. In the case of Shankaria vs State of Rajasthan, reported in AIR 1978 SC 1248, the Supreme Court of India held: 

 "It is well settled that confession, if voluntarily and truthfully made, is an efficacious proof of guilt. Therefore, when in a capital case the prosecution demands a conviction of the accused, primarily on the basis of his confession recorded under section 164, CrPC, the Court must apply a double test: 

 (2) If so, whether it is true and trustworthy? Satisfaction of the first test is a sine qua non for its admissibility in evidence. If the confession appears to the Court to have been caused by any inducement, threat or promise as is mentioned in section 24, Evidence Act, it must be excluded and rejected brevi manu. In such a case, the question of proceeding further to apply the second test, does not arise. If the first test in satisfied, the Court must before acting upon the confession, reach the finding that what is stated therein is true and reliable." 

 51. Considered in the light of the decision cited above, it is safe to conclude that the confessional statement neither fits with the prosecution version of the event nor does it corroborate the testimony of the prosecution witnesses and on this score, the confessional statement cannot be taken to be true. In the absence of any other credible evidence by which the complicity of the appellant in the case can be established, his conviction becomes equally unsustainable and the same is liable to be set aside. 

 54. Let Hamidul be set at liberty, if not wanted in connection with any other case. 

 56. The order of conviction and sentence of imprisonment for life in respect of Ashraf Ali Sheikh is hereby set aside and he is directed to be set at liberty if not wanted in connection with any other case.
